verse.meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after the battle is set. They say the mind is restless, turbulent and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees it is hard to hold, but says practice and letting go can train it.
verse.for_you: Your mind will not settle, and that is the weight you carry right now. The mind cannot be forced into silence.
verse.try_today: Notice where your mind is gripping the outcome and let that go for one hour.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on the five causes behind every action.
verse.sanskrit: अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् । विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥
verse.line: Every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You're one of them.
verse.translation: The seat, the doer, the various instruments, the many kinds of effort, and fifth, providence: these are the five causes of every action.
verse.why: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.
verse.misuse: Not 'it wasn't my fault'. You own your part; you just aren't the only cause.

prasang.title: What makes an action happen
prasang.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.
prasang.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that every action rests on five causes. These are the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You are only one of these five causes. The action happens because all five come together, not because you alone make it happen. This means you own your part, but you do not own the whole result.
verse.for_you: You are carrying the weight of the whole outcome in your head, as if the work succeeds or fails only because you do. You are one cause among five. Your part is the effort you put in, not the final result.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when you catch yourself owning the result, and name the other causes silently.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the center of a room where five threads pull the action, not one.
asks: What are the other four causes in my current situation?
How do I stop feeling like the whole result is on me?
Where do I see the unseen cause at work today?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: नैव प्रार्थयते लाभं नालाभेनानुशोचति । धीरस्य शीतलं चित्तममृतेनैव पूरितम् ॥
verse.line: Not begging for gain, not grieving loss: a steady mind stays cool and full.
verse.translation: He does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady one's cool mind is filled as if with nectar.
verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka from a place of finished teaching. He has walked through every corner of the mind and now offers its final shape. He says the wise do not beg for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady mind stays cool and full, as if it has been poured over with nectar. The point is that calm is not a prize you chase or a place you reach. It is the quality of your own ordinary holding.
verse.for_you: You are trying to rest before the work is done, as if your mind could settle only when the outcome is certain. The verse shows a mind that is already full, not because the work is finished, but because it does not beg for a different result.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when the mind asks for a different result, and let the body rest anyway.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own waiting room, and the mind refuses to be still until the future arrives.
asks: How do I stop begging for a different result?
Can I be calm without the future being certain?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu is teaching Nidagha how a person who is free inside moves through the world. Ribhu says you can be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. You can be a doer in the world, taking up what comes and doing the work at hand, while remaining a non-doer within. The mind stays clear and free of agitation even while you act fully. This is the way of someone who lives among others without being disturbed by what happens.
verse.for_you: Your mind is restless because you are trying to finish the work in your head before the day is done. The work is only on the outside. Let the doing be enough. Busy outside, unhurried inside.
verse.try_today: Notice when your hands are busy and your mind is still.
verse.scene_line: You are doing the work at hand while your mind stays clear.
asks: How do I let the outside busy-ness be enough?
How do I stop the mind from finishing the work?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: A seer speaks to you, saying this is the only way to live. You may wish for a long life, but the real work is how you do it. When you act with a spirit of letting go, your actions do not stick to you. They do not cling or bind you to the result. The idea is to hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone around you.
verse.for_you: Your work is yours to do. The results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop. You are caught in the loop of waiting for the outcome before you let yourself rest. The work is the only thing you control. Let the rest go.
verse.try_today: Pick one task and finish it without checking how it turns out.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own workshop, and the only thing to do is to work.
asks: How do I let go of the result?
How do I see myself in others at work?

story.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
story.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
story.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
story.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.
